levels.0: Lists 'send notifications' without separating transactional from marketing or asking about duplicates and provider failure.
levels.1: Names the three channels and that some messages are urgent, but leaves 'no duplicates' and the latency target vague.
levels.2: States transactional vs bulk with a numeric latency target (accepted under 200 ms, at the provider within seconds during a burst), zero loss after 202, a precise duplicate guarantee, preferences, quiet hours and per-user caps, and puts the in-app inbox out of scope.

levels.1: Uses 1B a day but ignores the 5× campaign bursts.
levels.2: Uses 1B a day, 200M users and 5× bursts, and notes campaigns are scheduled so capacity can be pre-scaled.

criteria.title: Rates per channel against provider limits

levels.1: Derives about 11.6k/s average and 58k/s peak but not per channel.
levels.2: Splits by channel (for example 51.5k/s push, 5.8k/s email, 580/s SMS at peak), compares each with the provider limit and concludes the providers are the bottleneck, which motivates reserved quota.

criteria.title: Storage, log write rate and worker sizing

levels.2: Sizes preferences (~40 GB), dedup keys (~100 GB for 24 h), the log (~500 GB a day, write rate ~35k/s), and sizes worker pools by provider latency ÷ concurrency with ρ below 0.8 at peak.

levels.0: A send endpoint with no idempotency.
levels.1: Mentions an idempotency key but not its scope, TTL or conflict behaviour.
levels.2: POST returns 202 with a notification id; a required, caller-scoped Idempotency-Key returns the same id on retry and 409 on a different body; includes priority, category, template id and version, and expires_at; plus campaign, cancel, preferences, devices and status endpoints.

levels.0: One database for everything with no reasoning.
levels.1: Picks reasonable stores without tying them to access patterns.
levels.2: Wide-column log with TTL keyed by notification id and by (user, month); preferences and devices by user id behind a cache; templates and campaigns in a relational store; dedup and caps in Redis with TTLs, with the consequence of losing Redis stated.

criteria.title: Pipeline with separate lanes and per-channel senders

levels.1: API → queue → workers → providers, one shared queue.
levels.2: Accept API → transactional and bulk topics → routers (preferences, dedup, render) → per-channel queues → sender pools → providers, with status to the log, retry queues, a DLQ, campaign fan-out and provider webhooks, each request type walked through.
Separate lanes, reserved provider quota per lane (token buckets), and bulkheaded worker pools; explains why a priority field on one FIFO log fails and what to alert on (oldest-message age).

levels.1: Backoff and a DLQ, but all errors treated the same.
levels.2: Classifies permanent, throttled and transient errors; backoff with jitter until expires_at; non-blocking retry queues; DLQ with owner and redrive; circuit breaker per provider; transactional fails over to a second provider while bulk waits.

Idempotency key at accept, idempotent stages on (notification id, channel), and an explicit per-category policy for the in-doubt provider timeout (collapse ids for push, retry OTPs, do not retry marketing SMS), measured as a metric.

criteria.title: Preferences, quiet hours, caps and kill switch

levels.1: Preferences and quiet hours, checked at accept time.
levels.2: Checks at routing time so opt-outs stop in-flight campaigns; quiet hours via a scheduled store with jittered release; per-user marketing caps that suppress; a campaign kill switch.

levels.1: Lists failures without detection or mitigation.
levels.2: Covers provider slow or down, sender crash in doubt, Redis and broker loss, AZ loss with N+1 sizing, poison messages and wrong-segment campaigns; at 10× names provider limits first, then dedup memory and log volume, with concrete changes.

States each decision with its alternative and the deciding reason (lanes vs priority field, late preference checks, effectively-once inside, 3 AZs at N+1) and names the key metrics: oldest-message age per lane, provider error rate, in-doubt count, DLQ growth.
